midnat.explanation: "Midnat" means "midnight". Do not mix it up with "middag" (dinner). To say what time you eat dinner, use it for the meal: "Vi spiser middag klokken seks" (We eat dinner at six).

midt.explanation: "Midt" means "in the middle". To say where the middle of a place is, use "midt i" (in the middle of): "midt i byen" (in the middle of town). To say the middle of a part of the day, use "midt på" (in the middle of): "midt på dagen" (in the middle of the day).

mig.explanation: "Mig" means "me". When you are the one doing the action, use "jeg" (I) instead: "Jeg ser ham" (I see him). When you do something to yourself, "mig" means "myself": "Jeg vasker mig" (I wash myself). After "til" (to) and "med" (with), use "mig" too: "til mig" (to me), "med mig" (with me).

mild.explanation: "Mild" means "mild". To talk about the weather, use it for a season: "Vinteren er mild i år" (The winter is mild this year). To talk about food that is not strong, use it for a food: "en mild ost" (a mild cheese).

militær.explanation: "Militær" means "military". When you talk about the armed forces as a whole, add "-et" to make the noun: "militæret" (the military). To say someone serves in them: "Han er i militæret" (He is in the military).

million.explanation: "En million" means "a million". English never adds an ending to "million" after a number, but Danish does. To say two million, use: "to millioner mennesker" (two million people). Do not mix it up with "en milliard" (a billion, which is 1,000 million). To say how much money, use: "en milliard kroner" (a billion kroner).

min.explanation: "Min" means "my". To say my car, use it with one car: "min bil" (my car). With one house, use "mit" instead: "mit hus" (my house). With more than one thing, use "mine": "mine børn" (my children).

related.en: your (with one thing like a car)

mindre.explanation: "Mindre" means "less". When you describe the size of a thing, it means "smaller": "et mindre hus" (a smaller house). Do not mix it up with "mindst" (least): "Hun har mindst penge" (She has the least money).

mindst.explanation: "Mindst" means "least". To ask who has the smallest amount of something, use it before the thing: "Hvem har mindst tid?" (Who has the least time?) To give the lowest number that is fine, use it before a number, where it means "at least": "mindst fem" (at least five).

mine.explanation: "Mine" means "my". When you talk about more than one thing, use it: "mine huse" (my houses). With one house, use "mit" instead: "mit hus" (my house). With one book, use "min" instead: "min bog" (my book).

minigolf.explanation: "Minigolf" means "mini golf". Unlike the English spelling, Danish has no space inside "minigolf".

minimal.explanation: "Minimal" means "minimal". Its opposite is "maksimal" (maximum). To say the highest speed that is possible, use the opposite: "maksimal hastighed" (maximum speed).

misfornøjet.explanation: "Misfornøjet" means "dissatisfied". It is built from "mis-" and "fornøjet" (pleased). The start "mis-" also works like English "mis-" in "at misforstå" (to misunderstand).

misforstået.explanation: "Misforstået" means "misunderstood". It comes from the verb "at misforstå" (to misunderstand). To call a feeling or loyalty misguided, use it too: "misforstået loyalitet" (misguided loyalty).

misinformation.explanation: "Misinformation" means "misinformation". Do not mix it up with "desinformation" (disinformation). Misinformation is false information spread by mistake: "Det er misinformation" (That is misinformation). Disinformation is false information spread on purpose: "Det er desinformation" (That is disinformation).

mistillid.explanation: "En mistillid" means "distrust". It is built from "mis-" and "tillid" (trust). To talk about a vote of no confidence in a government, use "et mistillidsvotum": "Der er et mistillidsvotum mod regeringen" (There is a vote of no confidence against the government).

mistænkelig.explanation: "Mistænkelig" means "suspicious". Do not mix it up with "mistænksom" (suspicious of others). To say a thing seems wrong, use "mistænkelig": "en mistænkelig lyd" (a suspicious sound). To say a person does not trust others, use "mistænksom": "en mistænksom nabo" (a neighbor who distrusts others).

mistænksom.explanation: "Mistænksom" means "suspicious". Do not mix it up with "mistænkelig" (looking suspicious). To say a person does not trust others, use "mistænksom": "en mistænksom nabo" (a neighbor who distrusts others). To say a thing seems wrong, use "mistænkelig": "en mistænkelig lyd" (a suspicious sound).

mistænkt.explanation: "Mistænkt" means "suspected". To name the person the police are looking at, use the noun "en mistænkt" (a suspect): "Politiet har en mistænkt" (The police have a suspect).

misundelig.explanation: "Misundelig" means "envious". To say who you envy, add "på" (of): "Han er misundelig på sin kollega" (He is envious of his coworker).

misundelse.explanation: "En misundelse" means "envy". Do not mix it up with "jalousi" (jealousy), the fear of losing a partner to someone else. To talk about that fear, say: "Jalousi kan ødelægge et forhold" (Jealousy can ruin a relationship).

misvisende.explanation: "Misvisende" means "misleading". The start "mis-" also appears in "at misforstå" (to misunderstand) and "mistillid" (distrust).

mit.explanation: "Mit" means "my". Use it with one thing that takes "et", as in "mit værelse" (my room). With one car, use "min" instead: "min bil" (my car). With more than one thing, use "mine": "mine børn" (my children).

related.en: your (with one thing like a room)

mod.explanation: "Mod" means "toward". To point to a direction, use it before the place: "Han går mod døren" (He walks toward the door). When you play an opponent, it means "against": "Danmark spiller mod Norge" (Denmark plays against Norway). To say you are against an idea, use "imod" (against) instead: "Jeg er imod det" (I am against it).

mode.explanation: "Mode" means "fashion". Do not mix it up with "en måde" (a way). To say a good way to learn, say: "Det er en god måde at lære på" (That is a good way to learn).
